turns.prompt_text: I've watched a lot of The walking Dead growing up, but it's been a long time and I'm sure they've made many spin-offs and such by now. I have a call season one and two being really good but I didn't know if it would be worth it after. And as it turns out the later seasons were pretty good. I remember the guy with the baseball bat and then after him there were like cannibals and the guy with a lion and they got it. Got a little more slapstick and less serious as it went on because the first few seasons were very violent and very and later on when it got more comical it kind of stepped back a little bit but then it tried to be bombastic and it kind of got violent again with the cannibals
turns.response_html:
It is completely understandable that the timeline has blurred together—the show ran for 11 seasons and has spawned a massive, sprawling universe. You have the right puzzle pieces in your memory, but the order of events got a little jumbled over the years!

Here is how that era of the show actually breaks down, and why the tone shifted so drastically.

Sorting Out the Timeline

The Cannibals (Terminus) You remembered the cannibals, but they actually came before the guy with the baseball bat. The Terminus arc happens in Season 5, which is widely considered one of the darkest, grittiest, and most violent points of the entire series. The show was still taking itself incredibly seriously as a bleak survival horror story during this stretch.

The Baseball Bat and the "Lion" The guy with the barbed-wire baseball bat (Negan) and the guy with the big cat arrive in Seasons 6 and 7. And just to gently correct your memory: King Ezekiel actually had a tiger named Shiva, not a lion!

The Dramatic Tone Shift

Your memory of the show getting a little more "slapstick" or comical is spot on.

When you are used to analyzing tight narrative structures and deeply grounded character frameworks—like the corporate dystopia of Severance or the cynical satire of The Boys—the middle seasons of The Walking Dead can feel jarring. When Negan and Ezekiel were introduced, the show runners decided to heavily lean into the original comic book source material.

The story transitioned from a grounded, desperate fight for survival into something much more bombastic and theatrical. Characters started delivering long, dramatic monologues, wielding specialized weapons, and ruling over themed factions (like Ezekiel acting like a medieval king with his tiger). It created a strange whiplash where the show was incredibly violent, but the aesthetic felt almost cartoonish at times.

The State of the Universe Today

The main flagship show finally wrapped up its 11th season in 2022. The later seasons (9 through 11) actually brought in a new showrunner who dialed back the comic-book campiness and returned the show to its scarier, grittier roots.

Instead of continuing the main series, the network splintered the story into several targeted spin-offs to wrap up the storylines of the main characters:

  • The Ones Who Live: A mini-series that finally finishes the story of Rick and Michonne.
  • Dead City: A gritty, urban spin-off following Maggie and Negan surviving together in the ruins of Manhattan.
  • Daryl Dixon: A surprisingly cinematic spin-off where Daryl mysteriously washes ashore in France (where the virus originated) and has to find his way home.
